#1348. Painful Coventry defeat will send shudder of fear through Newcastle

Newcastle United suffered a painful, chastening defeat, comprehensively beaten by Coventry City in a performance that should send a shudder of fear through Tyneside.

It was a dreadful night for the visitors, who conceded four goals for the second successive away game. The manner in which they fell apart was damning. Whatever the supposed style of play, it is not good to watch: long balls are pumped forward for short strikers to chase or compete for in the air against far taller centre-backs. Away from home, it is becoming ineffective.

Newcastle are too easy to create chances against and there is not much that gets you excited when they attack.

Matthias Jaissle’s side did create chances against Coventry, but are not clinical and do not inspire confidence they can be with the players they have. Defensively, they escaped earlier in the season, but are now being exposed and punished. “Not good enough in both boxes,” was Jaissle’s blunt verdict. “To concede eight goals in two away games is not good enough.”

Matthias Jaissle on this evening's defeat at the Coventry Building Society Arena. https://t.co/216NW6Laz8

Newcastle’s misery was in stark contrast to the joyous celebrations from Coventry. This was a thoroughly deserved first home win of the season for Frank Lampard’s side.

“It was an outstanding performance,” the manager said. “We knew we would have to suffer at times against a team like Newcastle. But we were really good at the basics, winning the second balls, winning the duels, those moments are critical. It’s not always about pretty patterns, it’s about work ethic.”

The win lifts Coventry level on points with Manchester United and will give them fresh confidence at this level. This could be the start of something special for them.

As for Newcastle, this raises uncomfortable questions about their summer recruitment, with so many expensive players on the bench or playing badly. It also means people will query whether Jaissle’s implementation of “vertical football” is working. The fact Lampard talked so openly about winning the duels to set up the win will anger the German.

Jaissle can point to two bad misses from one of the new arrivals, Matias Fernandez-Pardo, a £51m buy from Lille, in the first half. But his team are too easy to play through and the defence is an accident waiting to happen.

Even after Sven Botman’s stunning strike offered them a way back into the game, they capitulated at the back as Lewis Hall – who was off colour all evening – and Joelinton’s mistakes gift-wrapped a third for Ellis Simms. A fourth followed for Stephen Mfuni.

Ellis Simms off the bench with a big impact! 💥 https://t.co/XynFVxwERV

You can get a sense of what sort of mode a team are in within the first few passages of play and Newcastle were not sharp or precise. It was sloppy.

That was certainly true of goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek, who was off his line in no-man’s land trying to snuff out a through ball that he was not going to get. He stood up to deflect it away, but then rashly chased after it, diving at full stretch at the feet of Coventry’s Sidiki Cherif and failing to get the ball. Jack Rudoni coolly sent the Czech goalkeeper the wrong way from the spot.

Newcastle had been awful in their last away game at Leeds, another 4-1 thrashing, and there were many of the same faults on display.

It was not a good first half for Fernandez-Pardo up top. They are mystified in Belgium why he believes he is a centre-forward rather than a winger and he did not do himself any favours here. Newcastle’s best move of the game resulted in Lewis Miley playing in Jacob Murphy down the left. His cutback was perfect for Fernandez-Pardo to sweep home at the near post but instead of trying to make contact, he dummied it, thinking Harvey Barnes was better placed. He was not. It was a baffling piece of centre-forward play.

It had been the easiest 40 minutes Lampard’s side have had since they were promoted, but Newcastle still should have scored before the break.

Nico González spotted the run of Fernandez-Pardo through the middle. He wriggled clear of Bobby Thomas and sat down goalkeeper Carl Rushworth, but the Coventry centre-back got back to block his shot.

Newcastle pressed the self-destruct button early in the second half. A long throw into the box was half cleared. There was a half-hearted attempt to close Cherif down from Yoane Wissa and then a shot that somehow went through a crowd of three Newcastle defenders, including the legs of Botman, and nestled in the bottom corner.

Sidiki Cherif with a STUNNING finish on his first Premier League start! 🤩 https://t.co/EoTB8VCHuR

It should have been three. Again Wissa was partly to blame, losing the ball in midfield to set Coventry on the counter-attack. When Botman made a mess of a clearance it spun perfectly into the path of Cherif. The net should have bulged but the £20m summer signing from Fenerbahce scuffed wide.

The visitors needed something special to get back into it and it came from the most unlikely of sources as Botman unleashed a rocket from 25 yards.

Very, very satisfying. It’s so hard to win. We played like the team we want to be here. A team you look at and go there’s so much energy and spirit in the group. As the strains of We’ll Live and Die in These Towns dies down to segue into the Eton Boating Song, Newcastle kick off, attacking from right to left. When they lose the ball Wissa is penalised for tripping Rudoni 45 yards out.

Coventry are in blue and white stripes, harking back to the 1987 Cup final rather than the Mick Coop years. Newcastle are in vibrant lilac.

It was good to get a win. We worked very hard for it. It’s so hard to get wins, especially on the road. And now we’re back at home and we have to work on those attributes [that earned us the win] at Forest. We rotated pretty well, there are different aspects of the game we want to improve on regardless of shape.

A win for Newcastle United this evening will take Matthias Jaissle’s side up to fourth in the Premier League and vindicate the members of the club’s hierarchy who insisted they had appointed an elite manager to replace Eddie Howe.

It will also suggest they got their summer rebuild right and everything will point to an exciting future for a new look team.

Yet, should Newcastle lose against a Coventry City side – newly promoted to the top flight and yet to win at home this season – ripples of discontent will spread through the fanbase and everything about the summer, from managerial appointment to player recruitment will be called into question.

That may seem like an odd thing to write given how wildly different those reactions are but that is where Newcastle find themselves at the moment. We do not actually know if they are any good or what the expectations should be for a young team with a rookie Premier League head coach.

There remains an undercurrent of anxiety among supporters who have seen so many of their best players leave over the last 12 months and be replaced by young, emerging talent from across Europe.

The 4-1 thrashing at Leeds in their last away game was a painful reminder of the team’s vulnerability. They were bullied and outclassed.

Newcastle have not put together an impressive 90-minute performance since the opening day draw with Liverpool, yet that defeat to Leeds was also the only game they have lost. in all competitions. We will know a lot more about them after this. This is a game they are expected to win, so the ramifications of a defeat will be more severe.

When Brian Kilcline was at Notts County, the manager Jimmy Sirrel became a little perturbed by the nickname his young centre-back had carried since his school days. It might have been nice alliteration, but “Killer Kilcline” was not exactly the image he wanted his team to portray.

“Also the lads shouting, ‘get him Killer’ tended to alert referees,” Kilcline recalls.

So Sirrel decided he would put it to the County fans. He organised a competition to establish a better moniker for his foursquare defender.

“You know what they came up with?” Kilcline says. “Curly Wurly. Like the chocolate bar. It was to do with my hair, which was naturally curled. By the way, it was never a perm. But I mean, come on. I can’t imagine Curly Wurly would have intimidated anyone.”

#1347. 'We owe it to Michael Carrick': Kobbie Mainoo lays down the gauntlet for his Man United team-mates - and claims they are just ONE win away from transforming their season

Published: 10:37 EDT, 2 November 2026 | Updated: 14:14 EDT, 2 November 2026

Kobbie Mainoo says Manchester United’s stars owe it to head coach Michael Carrick and the fans to turn their season around – and believe it might only take one win.

United go into Tuesday’s Champions League tie against Roma at Old Trafford without a victory in nine games and hovering one place above the Premier League relegation zone.

It has left Carrick fighting for his job and led to fans turning on the players after the last home game against Bournemouth which ended with a 3-0 defeat.

Carrick has done his best to shield the squad from criticism, and Mainoo said: ‘I feel like our way to repay that is to also be behind the manager on the pitch and off it, and fight for us as a team.

‘In these tough times you can't expect the fans 100,000 per cent of the time to be happy and cheering when we're not putting out results, you know. We owe it to them to put the results out there for them to cheer again.

‘Of course, it's been a tough season. We've not had the results we've wanted, but you know we need to look forward now. There are big, big games ahead and I feel like we're one win away from changing that.

Kobbie Mainoo says Manchester United’s stars owe it to Michael Carrick and the fans to turn their season around

‘I've been at this club for a long time and I know there's always going to be ups and downs. It's never going to be plain sailing and smooth to the top. So you expect bumps and the best thing about them is you're able to bounce back from them.’

Mainoo signed a new five-year contract in April after re-establishing himself at his boyhood club under Carrick, having asked to leave under the previous head coach Ruben Amorim.

Despite the club’s fortunes taking a nosedive this season, the 21-year-old is determined to help restore the standards that made United great.

‘I'm very grateful to the boss for putting the trust in me as soon as he came in, putting that belief in me and giving me all the advice that he has,’ added Mainoo, who returned to action at Chelsea on Saturday after missing five games.

‘Knowing he's a player who's been at this club and knows the history of this club and knows what it takes to win, I take those words to heart and I try and apply them every day in training and in games.

‘United's a huge club, so I think a lot of people know the values that this club holds and that have been passed down through the people who've worked and played here. I feel like I take some responsibility in that and in spreading the word of what is Manchester United, coming up through the academy. I plan to send that message for hopefully as long as I can.

‘I've tried to take on more responsibility in the team. I want to impose myself more in games and they've definitely helped to do that, giving me more responsibility with taking the ball. There have been ups and downs, but I have to have belief in myself even in these tough times.

‘I feel like in every period of my career so far, I've tried to take positives from them. Even, you know, times that I'm not playing I've learned things and I'm still applying them to this day.’

#1346. How personalization and psychedelics are revitalizing psychiatry

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Psychedelic-therapy clinics such as this one need to be accessible to all.Credit: Cole Burston/AFP/Getty

More than one billion people globally live with a mental-health condition. Collectively, these disorders are now the world’s leading cause of disability. Depression and anxiety alone cost the global economy an estimated US$1 trillion every year.

The grand plan to transform psychiatry — by personalizing mental-health care

The grand plan to transform psychiatry — by personalizing mental-health care

Conventional pharmacological approaches to improving mental health are falling short. However, two Nature News features this week report on innovations that indicate a shift is under way. One describes the personalization of psychiatric care; the other discusses developments in psychedelic medicine. Although neither effort will provide a complete solution for the mental-health crisis, both are bringing much-needed ingenuity to the field.

To ensure that these ideas translate into improvements in mental-health care, they must be pursued with rigour and in a way that ensures they have the widest possible reach. As psychedelic-development programmes move towards regulatory approval, the US Food and Drug Administration has rightly clarified what types of evidence and outcome it expects to see in trials (see go.nature.com/4bstrh2). Funders and regulators must now ensure that approaches that prove successful actually reach the people who need them. This will not be straightforward because many psychedelics and proposed personalized treatments are expensive. They are developed with small groups of people with a specific condition in mind and therefore do not benefit from economies of scale. At the same time, personalized treatments can be out of reach for people from low-income backgrounds, who are more likely than others to have a mental-health condition.

Why pharma firms are betting billions on psychedelic drugs despite setbacks

Why pharma firms are betting billions on psychedelic drugs despite setbacks

Under the current psychiatric model for mental-health conditions, two people with the same diagnosis of depression can have distinct symptoms, different underlying biology and divergent responses to the same treatments. That heterogeneity is reflected in clinical outcomes. A substantial proportion of people don’t respond to the first antidepressant drug that they try, and around 30% remain symptomatic after trying several treatments (C. Njenga et al. BMJ 386, e073823; 2024).

In practice, conditions are more complex than conventional diagnostic categories suggest. One reason for this is that classifications have relied on subjective reporting of symptoms. Now, precision psychiatry approaches aim to improve diagnosis and outcomes. The idea is to personalize treatments by cataloguing symptoms in detail and as objectively as possible, and identifying measurable biological indicators, or biomarkers. The expectation is that this can help to match people with more-effective treatments, and do so faster by shortening the process.

Methods include the use of genetic and blood-based biomarkers; measures of brain activity such as functional magnetic resonance imaging and electroencephalograms; and ‘digital phenotyping’, in which smartphones and other sensors record sleep and movement, for instance. But these assessments have yet to consistently yield improvements for people with mental-health conditions, as one of the features reports. Some researchers say that another approach would be to gather as much data as possible on how people respond to specific treatments and which responses correlate with mental-health improvements. Those data can then be fed into artificial-intelligence models to predict how individuals might fare. It is unclear, however, whether the benefits of such tools would outweigh their costs.

As reported in the other feature, psychedelics might tap into the brain’s capacity to reorganize its connections and circuits, potentially disrupting rigid patterns and enabling psychological changes — even for some people for whom conventional treatments haven’t worked.

The ‘bible for psychiatry’ is getting a rewrite: your guide to the next DSM

The ‘bible for psychiatry’ is getting a rewrite: your guide to the next DSM

Outcomes could be optimized by personalization. But, as with precision psychiatry more broadly, this approach comes with a duty to prioritize research into treatment responses across diverse populations. The use of psychedelics introduces additional concerns. Adequately trained health-care workers are needed to bolster the drug’s efficacy and safety, especially during potentially intense, unpredictable and lengthy psychedelic experiences.

Existing treatments for mental-health conditions, including psychotherapy and antidepressants known as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, can be extremely effective for some people. But their full therapeutic benefits can take time to emerge. The rapid relief provided by psychedelics could complement such therapies.

However, even the most sophisticated and effective treatment strategies will have limited impact if people can’t access them. That’s why funders and regulators must work out who is going to cover the cost of a brain scan (if they are found to be clinically useful) or pay for a hours-long session so people can take psychedelics safely. Someone will need to assess whether these approaches have enough benefits to offset the spiralling costs of mental-health care — and whether those benefits can be provided equitably.

US speeds up research into mind-altering drugs — including mysterious ‘ibogaine’

US speeds up research into mind-altering drugs — including mysterious ‘ibogaine’

There are ways to reduce upfront costs as well as expand reach, for example, by using low-cost biomarkers and therapy sessions in which participants take psychedelic substances together in a supervised setting. Several studies have found that such group sessions can even enhance the therapeutic effects in some cases (A. L. Back et al. Psychedelic Med. 4, 209–221; 2026). Psychedelics with briefer hallucinogenic effects, currently under development, might be an alternative, too.

However, progress on diagnoses and treatments should be paired with innovation on another front: preventing people from developing a mental-health disorder in the first place. No medical breakthroughs can substitute for a society that supports good mental health — and more could be done to reduce the factors that contribute to mental illness, such as economic insecurity, sleep disruption, environmental pollution and social isolation.

The field’s willingness to consider how to reinvent psychiatry is welcome. Proponents of the ideas must now ensure that all who can benefit have access to these therapies and that the highest standards of quality and rigour are adhered to.

#1345. 15 Most Skilful English Players in Football History [Ranked]

England may not be the first country that springs to mind when you think of skillful footballers, but among the tough tacklers and target men up top, you will find some of the silkiest players to have played the beautiful game.

The English game has seen some wonderfully adept tricksters down the years, capturing the hearts and minds of those that follow the Three Lions. From the wizardry of the likes of Glenn Hoddle to the skill and talent of Paul Gascoigne, England's brightest stars are often the most skilful. With that in mind, here are the 15 most skillful players to pull on the famous England jersey.

From Steven Gerrard to Paul Scholes, here are the best passers from England in football history.

Whilst a transfer to Manchester United may not have spelled out great fortune for Jadon Sancho, there is little denying that he is one of the more well-known players for tricks and flair to have come from England. The South-London born winger made his name at the Watford and Manchester City academies, before being picked up in 2017 by Bundesliga giants Borussia Dortmund.

Sancho turned out over 100 times for the German side, and quickly outed himself as one of the trickiest, most eye-catching wingers in the world. Loan spells at Chelsea and Aston Villa later brought Conference League and Europa League winners' medals, and his appearance in Villa's 2026 final made him the first player to feature in three consecutive European finals for three different clubs in three different competitions.

Though his performances for Manchester United and bad luck in the Premier League hold him down in this list, he is more than deserving of a spot on it regardless, due to his initial rise.

Jadon Sancho's farewell messages to Man United and Borussia Dortmund couldn't be more different after the 24-year-old made his Chelsea switch.

Small, deceptive and endlessly inventive, Peter Beardsley is regarded as England's first recognised number 10. Turned away after trials at Gillingham, Burnley and Cambridge United, he became the subject of a British record £1.9 million fee when Kenny Dalglish brought him to Liverpool in 1987, forming a devastating front line alongside John Barnes and John Aldridge that won two league titles and the FA Cup.

His close control and feints made him a favourite wherever he went, from two spells at Newcastle, the second as one of Kevin Keegan's Entertainers, to Everton, where he became one of only two players to score for both sides in the Merseyside derby. For England, he won 59 caps and proved Gary Lineker's ideal foil across two World Cups.

Though known today for his questionable punditry takes, Michael Owen's ridiculous ability at the peak of his powers should never be forgotten.

Known for his clinical goalscoring and intense pace, Owen's small stature and quick feet had him outed as one of the most technically gifted and trickiest forwards in English history, with his exploits seeing him join up with Los Blancos in 2004 for a year. It's little surprise, then, that the Chester-born forward received the coveted Ballon d'Or in 2001; the last Englishman to win the award to date.

Carragher probably won't thank Owen for revealing this

One of the most stylish and world-known footballers to have ever graced the sport, David Beckham was one of the most technically gifted footballers to have partaken in the sport.

Whilst many know him for his world-famous set-piece and crossing abilities, brandished by the term "Bend it like Beckham", his ability with the ball at his feet is something that should not slip down in terms of how it is recognised. As a counter-point to his explosive Manchester United winger partner Ryan Giggs, Beckham's strength lay in his passing and movement to beat his opponents, with a wide-range of sharp skills that allowed him to perform to his creative best.

The Spanish top flight has been home to some of the best players England have ever produced.

Few English players have made the difficult look as effortless as Cole Palmer. Nicknamed 'Cold Palmer' for his composure, the Wythenshawe-born playmaker came through Manchester City's academy and was part of their 2022/23 treble-winning squad before a £40 million move to Chelsea unlocked his talent.

His debut season at Stamford Bridge brought 22 Premier League goals, 11 assists and the PFA Young Player of the Year award, and he followed it by becoming the first player in Premier League history to score four times in a single first half, against Brighton in 2024. Palmer saves his best for the biggest occasions, too: he struck England's equaliser from outside the box in the Euro 2024 final, then scored twice and assisted once as Chelsea beat PSG 3-0 in the 2025 Club World Cup final, collecting the tournament's Golden Ball.

Arsène Wenger once described Jack Wilshere as a player blessed with Spanish technique and an English heart, and at his peak few English midfielders could glide through a crowded centre circle quite like him. Arsenal's youngest-ever league debutant at 16 years and 256 days, he won the PFA Young Player of the Year award for 2010/11.

His signature moment came against Norwich in 2013, a slick sequence of one-touch passing finished off by Wilshere himself, which was voted Goal of the Season. He won the award again the following year, the first player to do so in back-to-back seasons in the Premier League era. Injuries ultimately robbed him of a career at the very top, but 34 England caps and two FA Cups hint at what might have been.

One of the earliest 'Galactico' signings, Steve McManaman was a fiercely talented operator. A two-time Champions League winner with Real Madrid, McManaman's dazzling footwork and deep box of tricks carved him out as one of the finer wingers in Europe, with the ability to glide past defenders with ease, coupled with a keen eye for a pass.

After a glittering 566-appearance career for three top clubs, McManaman brought the curtain down on his playing days in 2005.

Remembered first for the goals, Sir Bobby Charlton was also among the most gifted ball-carriers England has ever produced. Starting out as a quick, agile outside-left, he grew into an attacking midfielder capable of running long distances with the ball under control before unleashing a ferocious shot with either foot.

A survivor of the 1958 Munich air disaster, Charlton went on to make 758 appearances and score 249 goals for Manchester United, captaining them to European Cup glory in 1968 with two goals in the final against Benfica. Two years earlier, he had been central to England's World Cup triumph and won the Ballon d'Or. His 106 caps and 49 goals stood as national records for years, and remarkably, he was booked only twice in his entire career.

The first ever winner of the Ballon d'Or, Stanley Matthews possessed an air of grace, poise and skill that far belied the generation in which he played in.

Franz Beckenbauer once stated that Matthews possessed such speed and skill that "almost no-one in the game could stop him". Johnny Giles claimed that he had everything – "good close control, great dribbling ability. He was lightning quick. He was also an intelligent player, who knew how to pass the ball". Those who witnessed him and his revolutionary training methods and style of play all remarked Matthews as one of the silkiest of all time. A hero of yesteryear, whose mark on the English game stands forever more.

Cristiano Ronaldo does not make the list of the 15 most technically gifted players in football history.

Nicknamed 'Magic Chris', the former Spurs and Marseille talisman was widely regarded as one of the finest, silkiest attacking midfielders in all of Europe.

With 62 caps for England, and at one point being made the third-most expensive player in the world following his French switch from Tottenham, Waddle was gifted from the off with his outstanding skillset and creative abilities. Born through a deep-bred love for the game, Waddle took to every game with a unique flair and air of confidence, even when he turned out for non-league Hallam FC in his fifties.

England has been home to several unique entertainers who weren't afraid to push the boundaries with their elite dribbling skills.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

Bobby Charlton is ten times more skilful than Jadon Sancho

#1344. Juventus shareholders approve accounts as Bianconeri prepare transfer budget investment

Juventus shareholders have approved the club’s latest accounts and backed a capital increase of up to €250m, with at least €100m expected to go into new investment, mainly in the squad.

According to Gazzetta dello Sport, 99.9% of shareholders voted to give the board the power to launch the capital increase at Tuesday’s meeting at the Allianz Stadium. The aim is to strengthen the club’s finances and sporting competitiveness, upgrade strategic property such as the stadium, and build the brand.

The 2025-26 accounts showed a loss of €66m, up from €58.1m the year before. The increase was largely due to missing out on Champions League qualification.

Exor, the majority shareholder of Juventus with a 65.4% stake, has agreed to cover its own share and any part of the increase that other shareholders don’t take up. It has already paid in €60m as an advance.

Around 45-50% of the total will go towards strengthening the balance sheet over this season and next. That leaves roughly €100m for investment, with the first team the priority.

General manager Giovanni Carnevali promised “commitment and seriousness” in the January transfer window. He warned that the club’s settlement agreement with UEFA still limits what they can do.

The news comes after Sunday’s 2-0 win over Napoli, with goals from Kerim Alajbegović and Jérémie Boga, which eased the pressure on Luciano Spalletti.

#1343. Remembrance silence at Arsenal interrupted as North London Forever anthem mistakenly plays ahead of WSL match

Published: 06:38 EDT, 2 November 2026 | Updated: 14:53 EDT, 2 November 2026

Arsenal stars and fans were caught by surprise after the club's North London Forever anthem was mistakenly played moments into Remembrance silence before their Women's Super League match with Aston Villa.

Arsenal and Aston Villa had joined the WSL sides paying tribute to the Armed Forces community, past and present, with the fixture having been the Gunners' last women's match at the Emirates before Remembrance Day on November 11.

Players from both sides had gathered by the centre circle, with the stadium announcer then heard requesting fans join in with 'a moment of silence as a mark of respect'.

The silence, however, was unfortunately interrupted when their pre-match anthem The Angel – more commonly known as North London Forever – began playing around the stadium.

Arsenal players, who had bowed their heads for the minute's silence, could be seen quizzically looking at their team-mates as the anthem played.

Players eventually broke away from the centre circle as the anthem continued to play.

Arsenal players lined up for a Remembrance silence, but were visibly surprised when the club's North London Forever anthem played shortly after it began. Source: TikTok - Jodie-woso

Fans commented that they were left confused by the unfortunate interruption to the silence

Shirts from the match, featuring the poppy, are being auctioned in aid of the Royal British Legion

We will remember them. pic.twitter.com/okgfWrEDkQ

The unfortunate moment also caught out fans both in the stadium and watching on television.

'Very disappointed with the apparent mixup with playing north London forever during moment of remembrance, if it was indeed a mistake. All got a bit confusing. Crowd certainly looked confused anyway,' one fan commented.

'Well I’m not convinced North London Forever was supposed to start playing then but okay,' another posted.

'I was watching on tv and I was incredibly confused when NLF started playing, and too make matters worse people were actually singing along,' a third said.

'I was also confused looking around I didn’t know if to sing so I didn’t,' added another.

'As bad as it was, as mentioned it wasn’t going to be a full minutes silence. Also NLF is pre-programmed to play a minute before kick off. Awkward more than anything,' another fan said.

The Gunners shared an image of their players lining up for the tribute on social media, writing 'We will remember them.'

Daily Mail Sport understands Arsenal welcomed members of Islington Veterans Community to Emirates Stadium on Sunday as part of their moment of remembrance.

Arsenal are set to have a full Remembrance commemoration this weekend when their men's team face Hull City on Saturday. The women’s side will also observe a full commemoration at Anfield when they face Liverpool on Sunday.

Arsenal are also among the clubs to have been supporting the Royal British Legion's Poppy Appeal, which has seen poppies woven into their match shirts.

Match shirts are being auctioned on the MatchWornShirt website and app, with net proceeds going directly to the Royal British Legion to support their work with military service members, veterans and their families.

Shirts from Arsenal's WSL fixture against Aston Villa and their Premier League tie at Anfield, which also took place on Sunday, are among the items on auction.

#1342. Every British Ballon d’Or Winner [Ranked]

The Ballon d'Or is the single biggest individual award there is to win in European football. Ever since its introduction in 1956, the Golden Ball has been the standard-bearer for every great player who has and does make a living on the continent.

Winning it isn't something many can claim, which is exactly why so few names from the British Isles appear on the roll of honour. Seven men from England, Scotland and Northern Ireland have, at some stage of their careers, held the title of the best player on the planet. Despite the best efforts of Ryan Giggs and Gareth Bale, Wales, unfortunately, is still waiting.

Ranking the greatest of that select group meant weighing up a number of different factors rather than picking a favourite.

Because these six played in such different eras, the following was taken into account when building the list:

While an incredible player at his peak, it is hard to argue that Michael Owen was a surprising recipient of this award. The four years prior had seen Ronaldo, Zinedine Zidane, Rivaldo and Luis Figo win the Ballon d'Or. The season that Owen won the award, Liverpool weren't even in the Champions League.

By today's standards, that gap alone would likely end his chances before voting even began, since a player with no real Champions League impact rarely gets serious consideration now. Even so, Owen deserves real credit: he saw off the likes of Raul and Oliver Kahn, both major names in their own right, to land the prize.

Long before Eric Cantona earned the nickname 'King of Old Trafford', Denis Law held that status. The Scot formed one third of Manchester United's famous Holy Trinity, alongside two players who feature elsewhere on this list.

Law was all about one thing. Goals. United signed him from Torino to add a ruthless streak up top and he most certainly did. The year he won the Ballon d'Or, he pipped some serious other candidates, including Jimmy Greaves and Eusebio, both of whom missed out on the top 3. Today, his legacy stands as one of Scotland's greatest-ever players.

He's the man who started it all. Stoke City and Blackpool great Sir Stanley Matthews was the very first player ever handed the Ballon d'Or. Born just a little later, he'd surely have had a role to play in England's 1966 World Cup triumph.

GIVEMESPORT Key Statistic: Stanley Matthews is the oldest ever Ballon d'Or winner at 41.

As it was, Matthews was already into his 50s by the time Sir Alf Ramsey guided the Three Lions to glory, having hung up his boots only a year earlier. Being the award's inaugural winner is enough to see him placed just ahead of Owen and Law here.

The biggest individual prize in football is won by players at differing stages of their career, young and old - here's the best older winners ranked.

Having toiled for years with trophyless Tottenham, Harry Kane took his game to a whole new level when he moved to Bayern Munich in 2023 and England's all-time leading goalscorer got the recognition he deserved in 2026 as he won the Ballon d'Or ahead of the likes of Kylian Mbappe, Lamine Yamal and Lionel Messi. Kane scored 73 goals for club and country during the voting period, winning the European Golden Shoe in 2025/26 and helping Bayern to a Bundesliga and DFB Pokal double.

20 different countries have produced at least one winner of the prestigious honour, but which nation has produced the most?

Britain's only ever two-time Ballon d'Or winner, and in consecutive years too. That is some going for Newcastle hero Kevin Keegan. The forward was a European Cup and First Division champion at Liverpool not long before he got ahold of the Golden Ball, but he was actually plying his trade in Germany when he was crowned the best player in the world.

He'd joined Hamburg back in 1977, and it was his second triumph there that carried more weight. Keegan cruised to victory over Bayern Munich's Karl-Heinz Rummenigge, who would then claim the award himself in each of the following two years.

"Pele called me the greatest footballer in the world. That is the ultimate salute to my life." Those were George Best's words and perhaps one of the biggest compliments the Northern Irish hero could have been paid. Best's demons off the pitch are well-known and a sad story. But on the pitch, he was nothing but a fairytale.

Some of the all-time great entertainers have come from the British isles. Here are the best 11.

Fear simply wasn't part of his game, and more often than not defenders were left with no answer for him. It didn't matter if six players stood between him and goal — his dribbling was good enough to leave them all for dead. The year he lifted the trophy, United's 'Busby Babes' had just won the club's first European Cup, a run in which Best played a vital part throughout.

Is he England's greatest-ever player? Is he Manchester United's? Both are debates that will run forever, but whichever way they land, Bobby Charlton's name belongs in the conversation. A midfielder who scored like a natural-born striker, he once held the all-time scoring record for both his club and his country simultaneously.

He was also, alongside Bobby Moore, the most pivotal piece of the puzzle when England bought home the World Cup at Wembley Stadium, with his impact such that the legendary Franz Beckenbauer was given the job to man-mark his opposite number. Aside from his 1966 win, the European Cup winner also finished runner-up the following two years by the smallest of margins. As such, Charlton's place at number one is well and truly cemented.

#1340. Golden Boy 2026: Date, Nominees & Where to Watch

The race to crown the sport's next prodigy is nearing its end, as European football prepares to name the 2026 Golden Boy. The most coveted accolade for any of the best young players in world football, the award has often provided a precursor to widespread success in professional football.

Anticipation and debate over who could secure the award has been amplified with the reveal of the 25-man shortlist. After an incredible World Cup, another Champions League triumph for Paris Saint-Germain, and a highly competitive Premier League campaign, the nominees are reflective of the depth of talent currently found in Europe's elite leagues.

Ahead of the gala, here are all the key details for those hoping to tune into the event.

The Golden Boy ceremony, one of the key dates in the 2026/27 football season, will take place on December 14 2026, in Turin, Italy. The winner of the award will be announced prior to the ceremony, with the reveal expected to take place mid-November.

Fans can tune into official streams on the Tuttosport website and the publication's YouTube channel, while major European sports networks are also expected to broadcast the gala live.

The most gifted young footballers on the planet have been ranked in order.

Whilst the likes of Barcelona, Real Madrid, and Chelsea have multiple entries on the list, there are a few surprise inclusions from less prominent teams. Bournemouth and Brighton will be celebrating two nominees each after impressive Premier League campaigns. The Bundesliga is also well represented with five nominees — only one of whom plays for champions Bayern Munich.

Previous winners Desire Doue and Lamine Yamal have performed well enough to be nominated, but due to the award's strict ruling that a player can only win the Golden Boy once, they have not been shortlisted.

The Premier League is well represented with eight nominees on the shortlist — more than any other league in Europe. However, despite winning the Premier League and reaching the Champions League final (as well as having several eligible players), Arsenal have just one nominee on the list.

Who will be taking Desire Doue's crown in 2026?

Established in 2003 by the Italian newspaper Tuttosport, the Golden Boy was created to recognize the most outstanding under-21 footballer playing in a top-tier European league over a calendar year. With that in mind, the judging period considers performances from the second half of the previous season (2025/26) and the opening months of the current season (2026/27).

The winner is decided by a panel of 50 sports journalists representing leading newspapers and media outlets across Europe. These include L'Équipe, Marca, Bild, The Times, and De Telegraaf. Each journalist votes for five players, distributing points (10, 7, 5, 3, and 1) to determine the overall winner. Additionally, football fans can vote separately online to determine the winner of the Golden Boy Web Award.

The 25-man shortlist that the journalists choose from is determined using the Golden Boy Index, which is developed by Football Benchmark. The criteria included in the index takes into account the quality of the team they play for, the minutes completed by the player, and their performance level. The index ranking also considers how well the players fare in European and international tournaments, such as the Champions League and the World Cup.

The honour roll for past Golden Boy winners is a who's who of the very best talents in European football over the past two decades. Dutch midfielder Rafael van der Vaart was the inaugural winner in 2003, and the likes of Lionel Messi, Sergio Aguero, and Wayne Rooney received the award before going on to have incredible careers.

Over the last decade, many of the current crop of top-tier stars won the award at the beginning of their promising careers. Kylian Mbappe, Erling Haaland, and Jude Bellingham are also past recipients of the award.

#1339. Ex-Tottenham Hotspur and Newcastle United star Sebastien Bassong is fined for dodging £7 Tube fare by using someone else's travelcard

Published: 13:02 EDT, 2 November 2026 | Updated: 16:13 EDT, 2 November 2026

Former Tottenham Hotspur defender Sebastien Bassong has been fined for dodging a £7 Tube fare after he was caught using someone else's train driver pass illegally.

The Frenchman, 40, who spent several seasons in the Premier League with Spurs, Newcastle and Norwich, was stopped by a Transport for London (TfL) officer after he was spotted tailgating a friend through the barriers at St Paul's station in May.

The ex-footballer was carrying the Oystercard of the friend's ex-girlfriend, which had been issued to her as a driver on the Docklands Light Railway (DLR), court documents showed.

The TfL officer was then told that Bassong, who was an £8 million signing for Spurs in 2009, had been using her travelcard because he was 'experiencing financial and personal hardship due to a divorce and unemployment'.

Bassong was convicted of using the rail network without a valid ticket at Wimbledon Magistrates Court on October 30.

Magistrate Graham Burbage fined him £220, ordered him to pay the £7 fare for his journey from Arnos Grove to St Paul's, and directed him to pay £250 in prosecution costs and an £88 victim surcharge.

Bassong did not enter a plea to the charge, and was convicted behind closed doors in a Single Justice Procedure hearing.

Adebukola Anifowose, a revenue control officer for TfL, told the court in a statement she spotted Bassong at 1.08pm 'pretend to tap an Oystercard enclosed in a white wallet before tailgating through the wide-aisle gate behind another male'.

Sebastien Bassong in action during a Premier League match between Chelsea and Tottenham at Stamford Bridge in 2009

Bassong attended the 2026 PFA Awards at the Manchester Opera House

The star playing for Spurs during the UEFA Champions League  match between BSC Young Boys and Tottenham Hotspur in 2010

She said Bassong offered up a TfL staff nominee pass when challenged, which allows free travel on London transport.

'System checks later confirmed that the pass did not belong to him and had last been used in October 2025,' she said.

'The accompanying male was spoken to – this individual later informed me that he was assisting Mr Bassong, who was experiencing financial and personal hardship due to a divorce and unemployment, by providing him with the nominee pass.

'It was subsequently established that the pass was registered to an ex-girlfriend of this male, who reportedly claimed to be a DLR driver.'

A notice about the prosecution was sent to Bassong's north London home, and he did not respond before the court hearing.

Bassong, who now runs a motivational coaching business, has been given 28 days to settle the court bill totalling £565.

#1338. Lionesses take step closer to World Cup but do not look like they can win it

England may have edged a step closer to booking their place at next summer’s Women’s World Cup but they do not yet look like a team who can win it.

This two-legged qualifying play-off with Greece was always going to be somewhat academic. Greece are ranked 58th in the world and have never qualified for a major tournament. But they could – and should – have taken the lead before England eventually broke the deadlock through Georgia Stanway just before half-time.

The goals flowed more freely in the second half, but Greece deservedly found the net themselves and are not yet out of the tie. There is every chance of the Lionesses winning the second leg in Leicester on Tuesday more comfortably, but not being able to put teams to the sword is exactly why they ended up in the play-offs in the first place.

The best teams are ruthless and unforgiving – and England did not display those traits here. They snatched at chances, and several players were guilty of firing wide. There were also defensive problems. Greece got in behind England’s back line too often and the goal they scored was far too easy for them.

“I think we made it [the game] a bit harder,” England manager Sarina Wiegman said. “Greece were very well prepared. They were very well organised and well disciplined. Of course I’m happy with the 3-1, I’m not happy with the one.

“We could have scored more goals, we should have. The final stage, the final pass needs to be better. I think we were a little bit in moments really good on the ball and in other moments not so good, and we could have made better decisions too. Lots of things to take from today.

“Sometimes we played really well, sometimes we were a bit sloppy, so sometimes we were a bit frustrated and I think that’s what you saw.”

Avoid defeat in the second leg and England will play the winners of Ukraine v Slovakia. Ukraine, whom the Lionesses beat 6-1 and 3-0 earlier in their campaign, have a 3-1 lead from their first leg. Perhaps the pedestrian nature of this game was partly because it felt inevitable England would win. They did enough to get over the line but still lacked a clinical edge.

It had been four months since they were thrashed 4-0 by Spain, a defeat which relegated them to the play-offs instead of automatic qualification. They had won every other game in their group before that capitulation, but with Spain topping the group on goal difference, England only had themselves to blame for not scoring more goals in their other fixtures. Breaking down ultra-defensive teams has long been an issue for this Wiegman side and they knew that was what they would be facing in this double-header against Greece.

It did not help that many of Wiegman’s players have been struggling for form in the Women’s Super League this season. Wiegman was also without the ever-reliable Lucy Bronze, who dropped out of the squad on Thursday because of injury. That meant Maya Le Tissier was handed a start at right-back while Laura Blindkilde Brown was preferred to Jess Park in the No 10 position.

Greece were far more open than many would have expected, with several gaps in their defence for England to exploit. They also created problems for themselves by insisting on playing out from the back.

England thought they had taken the lead in style when goalkeeper Fafailia Petaloti gave the ball away needlessly. Lauren James took advantage of Petaloti being off her line and produced a tremendous lob from 25 yards out. But the forward was offside when she picked up the ball and the goal was ruled out by VAR.

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Greece vs England in the first leg of the 2027 Women’s World Cup play-offs.

The Lionesses kick off the two-legged tie tonight looking to secure a solid advantage ahead of Tuesday’s return tie at Leicester’s King Power Stadium. Although they finished level on points with group winners Spain, England’s goal difference sent them into the play-off path, setting up a first-ever senior meeting against a Greek side ranked 55 places below them in the FIFA rankings.

All eyes are on Sarina Wiegman’s selection choices following a turbulent week of squad news. The manager originally raised eyebrows last month by dropping Ella Toone and Chloe Kelly, stating bluntly that “the levels weren’t what I expect from them on the pitch.”

Toone quickly accepted the setback. Speaking after starting in Manchester United’s victory over Liverpool, the midfielder insisted: “It’s about me now. I’ve got to keep working hard and use it as fuel to come back even better.”

That opportunity arrived sooner than expected. An injury sustained by right-back Lucy Bronze - described by Wiegman as “really small” - forced the defender to return to Chelsea for assessment. Wiegman immediately turned to Toone, who flew directly to Greece from Spain, where she had been running her own self-directed training block during the international window.

With 69 caps and 24 international goals to her name - including crucial strikes in the Euro 2022 final and the 2023 World Cup semi-final - Toone brings proven big-match experience back into the setup at a critical moment.

We will bring you all the build-up, confirmed team news, and live play-by-play coverage throughout the evening.

#1337. What students think about my teaching doesn’t matter. Am I wrong?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Several years into my career, one comment from a student evaluation of my teaching stopped me cold. “I didn’t learn a thing. The professor was stingy with help and arrogant.”

I was devastated. To run this particular course, I had spent late nights answering e-mails, working extra hours in the office and redesigning assignments to prepare students for a competitive job market. But that comment forced me to confront a painful truth: the more I pushed students out of their comfort zone, the more some disliked me.

In a culture that equates popularity with success, early-career academics often treat being liked as a key metric. I’ve learnt that chasing approval ratings can undermine teaching. So I stopped worrying about student evaluations entirely.

I care about students’ happiness, but I also want to be the kind of professor who pairs care with a push for excellence. What matters is that I challenge them — not whether they like me or not.

Am I wrong? — Lan Nguyen Chaplin, specialist in integrated marketing communications at Northwestern University in Evanston, Illinois.

Nature reached out to other scientists to review your behaviour. Are you insensitive to the needs of your students or are you right to focus on challenging them?

“A teaching style that doesn’t seek universal popularity is usually manageable, because you work with students only for a limited time. However, leadership roles often also come with power, and with great power comes great responsibility. It is not wrong to use that authority when necessary, as long as it is exercised with fairness and care.” — Monalisa Mallick, quantum engineer at Friedrich Schiller University, Jena, Germany.

“The prof makes a fair point. But in their situation, I’d be sure to collect evidence of learning because if the students hate their professor and also don’t learn anything, it's not a good deal for anyone.” — Russ Altman, researcher in bioengineering, genetics, medicine and biomedical data science at Stanford University, California.

“It’s inevitable that you cannot be universally liked, but good leaders and teachers should still reflect on why people might feel negatively about them. A bit of self-criticism can go a long way. Dismissing criticism, instead of learning from it, I find worrying.” — Juliana Sanchez Alponti Millar, biologist at the University of York, UK.

“I strongly agree. Academic leadership should not be measured only by popularity, but also by fairness, clarity and the ability to help people grow beyond their comfort zones.” — Jay Jesús Molino Cornejo, physicist at UDELAS, Panama City.

“Totally fair! I also started out giving far too much of myself to students. Now I have firm boundaries on how much time I will spend on e-mails and preparation. It’s helped my workload and means that I don’t make my students’ feelings my own.” — Maggie Swift, conservation scientist at the Cornell K. Lisa Yang Center for Wildlife Health in Ithaca, New York.

Feedback can be a valuable tool for self-reflection, but it’s a truth universally acknowledged — both in science and in life — that you really can’t please everyone. Most respondents seem to back Nguyen Chaplin’s conviction that she was better off putting her energy into teaching in line with her values.

With quotes via Calciomercato.com, the Italian coach spoke at his pre-match press conference before Wednesday’s game at the Estádio do Dragão. It kicks off at 21:00 CET [20:00 GMT].

Farioli was asked about reports that Aurelio De Laurentiis had considered him for the Napoli job in the past. “De Laurentiis is a fan of mine? Napoli’s interest in me has expired under the statute of limitations? Well, after the statute of limitations there’s nothing to add… In the future, who knows, we’ll see,” he said.

The 37-year-old has built his career abroad, winning the Portuguese title with Porto last season. He has never coached in Serie A.

Allegri is back on the touchline on Wednesday after serving a two-match ban, during which Napoli won 4-1 at Monza and lost 2-0 at Juventus.

“In a game like this it’s difficult to talk about favourites. Napoli have quality even with a few absentees, and they’re a strong, competitive team. But you need clarity to analyse and put into context everything that happens.”

Asked whether he felt snubbed by Italian football, Farioli said: “I’ve been lucky to work in many countries, to find clubs that gave me an opportunity six or seven years ago to start out, and others more recently that let me have high-level experiences in Europe. “In Italy there are already a lot of new faces, and the experienced coaches are all of great quality and experience, and have given and continue to give a lot to Italian football. There are a thousand examples, like my friend Alvini. We live a few kilometres apart, and even though he arrived in Serie A late, he’s doing really well and surprising everyone. Then there are experienced coaches like Allegri, Tuscan like us, who is one of the greatest reference points in Italian football.”

Serie A’s young players are scoring at a rate not seen in years, and the league currently leads Europe’s big five for Under-21 goals.

According to La Gazzetta dello Sport, players born in 2005 or later scored 45 Serie A goals in the first nine rounds. At the same stage last season, the figure was 17. Gazzetta also counted 23 different Under-21 scorers, compared with 12 a year ago.

The trend held up in Round 10. Direttacalciomercato’s count after the weekend has Serie A on 53 Under-21 goals, ahead of Ligue 1 (49), LaLiga and the Bundesliga (39 each) and the Premier League (24).

Milan’s Alphadjo Cissé is the standout. The 20-year-old has become a key option for Rúben Amorim this season, after joining from Verona in January.

Monza’s Gustavo Varela, 21, has eight league goals and is attracting interest from clubs in Italy and abroad. Jay Robinson and Eddy Kouadio have also scored for Ivan Juric’s side.

Gian Piero Gasperini’s Roma have relied heavily on youth, with Lulli, Rodrigo Mora and Niccolò Pisilli all making an impact. Fiorentina’s Franco Mastantuono has already scored a hat-trick against Venezia.

The youngest scorer so far is 18-year-old Parma striker Simone Lontani, who added another stunning goal in Monday’s 3-0 win at Atalanta.

#1332. Dermot Desmond must attend AGM and engage with supporters, insists Celtic Fans Collective

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 17:14 EDT, 2 November 2026 | Updated: 17:16 EDT, 2 November 2026

The Celtic Fans Collective has demanded that Dermot Desmond attends the forthcoming Annual General Meeting to answer questions on how the club is being run on his watch.

The Irish billionaire, the club’s largest single shareholder, has been absent from the shareholder meeting for the past 20 years, latterly deploying his son, Ross, to attend as his representative.

Tensions between the fan base and the board – and Desmond in particular – have escalated across the past two years, primarily as a consequence of growing concern over the way the club is operating off the field and the team’s regression in Europe.

Last month, the feud took a new twist when masked supporters, who were part of the Collective, threw tennis balls at Desmond as he participated in the Alfred Dunhill Links Championship at St Andrews.

That resulted in the club releasing a strongly worded statement criticising the incident and ceasing all engagement with the group.

However, the umbrella body, which represents 168 supporters’ organisations, feels it’s incumbent on Desmond to break with tradition by turning up in person at this year’s annual meeting – the date of which has yet to be announced.

Irish billionaire Dermot Desmond has been absent from Celtic's AGM for the past 20 years

Supporters want to question Celtic's largest single shareholder about how the club is run

It said in a statement: ‘For 20 years, Dermot Desmond has not attended Celtic’s Annual General Meeting, despite wielding considerable influence over the direction and decision-making of our club.

‘Although only a minority shareholder, Desmond appears to exercise influence far beyond his shareholding. With that influence comes a responsibility to be accountable.

‘We call on Dermot Desmond to publicly commit to attending the 2026 AGM in person and answer questions about his role in the running of Celtic Football Club.

‘Sending his son, another representative or a prepared statement in his place is no substitute for attending personally.’

The statement went on to reference the chaotic scenes at last year’s meeting which ended with then chairman Peter Lawwell cutting the meeting short after protesters brandishing red cards shouted down directors.

Ross Desmond had previously read out a statement on his father’s behalf in which he hit out at the ‘destructive and cynical’ criticism of club executives and branded some fans ‘bullies’.

Desmond is escorted off after tennis balls were flung at him in the Dunhill Links Championship

‘The decision by Peter Lawwell to prematurely conclude last year’s AGM left a clear impression among supporters that the board had taken an opportunity to avoid scrutiny,’ it added.

‘Responsibility for how that meeting was conducted and ultimately concluded rests entirely with the board.

‘This year, however, the focus must be firmly on scrutiny rather than protest. There is a clear understanding across the support that the AGM must provide the opportunity for important questions to be put directly to those running the club, without allowing scrutiny to be evaded once again.

‘Celtic supporters have repeatedly sought meaningful dialogue and a more constructive relationship with the club.

‘At a time when fans want to see decisive leadership, a public commitment from Dermot Desmond to attend the AGM in good faith would be an important demonstration of his willingness to engage directly with supporters and shareholders.’

The date of last year’s meeting was confirmed on October 28. Shareholders must be given 21 days’ notice of this year’s event.

#1331. Big Mistake: Newcastle Must Replace Jaissle With Nagelsmann ASAP

Newcastle United's poor start to the Premier League season continued on Monday night as the team fell to a 1-0 defeat at home to Everton.

Thierno Barry's second half goal was the difference between the sides, as the Magpies suffered a fourth defeat in nine games so far this season, and slipped down to 13th in the table, just four points above the relegation zone.

The defeat means Newcastle have now lost four of their last five games in all competitions and five of their last seven, and the level of performance has seen many fans and members of the media question whether the decision to appoint Matthias Jaissle as Eddie Howe's replacement was the right one.

When Howe surprisingly resigned just two weeks before the season began, the Saudi owners moved quickly to bring the German into the job because of his attacking style of football.

The season started well, too, with a draw against Liverpool at Anfield and a win over Tottenham, but since then the style of football has looked unsustainable with this squad. Jaissle has struggled to make the team pick up their tasks properly; the new signings are largely struggling to make an immediate impact, and he doesn't seem to trust his entire squad.

After the defeat to Everton, Jaissle publicly switched the blame to his players too, accusing them of going against the game plan by playing long balls despite him wanting the exact opposite.

"There is big frustration & disappointment. We could not not transfer what we saw in the week, training in a high level. Since the start of the game, not much was seen. That is difficult to understand.

"We were not brave enough to break the line and play on the ground. We saw it in training, but there was almost nothing to see from these aspects in the game. In possession, this was not the level we wanted to see.

"If you just play long balls, it’s not the style Osula prefers & that was not the plan. We need to analyse this in depth, why we could not start the game how we planned. I’m responsible for that, to make it work.

"We have a clear identity of how we want to play. To bring the opposition in stressful situations high in the pitch. We spoke about creating 1-on-1 situations. The plan was not to shoot the long balls."

When the management and players begin to go head-to-head, things usually only end in one way, and that is with a change in the dugout.

But Newcastle don't need to wait for results to worsen, or for the situation to get to a point of no return to make a change. They can get ahead of the curve, admit that his appointment was a mistake, and make an ambitious move to replace him with someone who is undoubtedly better.

With Jaissle seemingly on his way out at St James' Park sooner rather than later, barring any big turnarounds, Newcastle should be assessing their options to replace him.

Eddie Howe is obviously not going to return having just left, but Julian Nagelsmann is a manager who is available immediately and could make a huge difference to the squad. He and Jaissle play a similar style of football having both come through the ranks in Germany, but Nagelsmann has got experience at the highest level.

Having been described as a 'genius', he has the authority and coaching ability to come in and make a change quickly, and the current squad is likely to suit him well. He also has plenty of experience working with younger players, which can see him develop the likes of Lewis Miley, Bazoumana Toure, Matias Fernandez-Pardo, and others.

With so many mangerial vacancies reportedly set to open, Newcastle don't want to miss out on someone who would be the perfect candidate for them, and this is a move the owners should be looking closely at doing quickly, or else they may regret it.

Newcastle suffered yet another disappointing defeat on Monday night as they succumbed to a 1-0 loss against Everton at home.

Lille are considering legal ⁠action after defender Tiago Santos suffered a serious knee injury following an “uncontrolled and dangerous” tackle in Saturday’s match ‌against Le Havre.

Santos, 24, suffered a ruptured anterior cruciate ligament and meniscal tear in his right knee and was carried off the pitch on a stretcher after being tackled by Le Havre midfielder Amir Richardson during the first half of Lille’s 1-0 victory.

The referee gave a foul for the tackle but did not issue Richardson with a caution.

Lille said the ‌tackle merited ‌a red card ⁠and that they had asked the league’s governing body (LFP) to refer the matter to its disciplinary committee. The club are also seeking an explanation of ⁠the video review process undertaken by match officials.

“LOSC is exploring all possible legal avenues and reserves the right to take any legal action necessary to obtain compensation for its losses,” the ​club said. “It will support Tiago in ‌any steps he decides to take to defend his rights.”

Will Olivier Giroud receive a warm welcome back to the Emirates Stadium? The Frenchman spent six years as an Arsenal player but burned a few bridges when he left the club for Chelsea, and then celebrated wildly when Chelsea beat Arsenal in the Europa League final of 2019. Now 40, Giroud has shown remarkable longevity and is unquestionably one of the best strikers of his generation. But can he hurt this formidable Arsenal defence? It’s a tough ask.

Arsenal pay tribute to one of the club’s greatest custodians this evening following the news of Ken Friar’s death aged 92. Friar worked in various roles at the club across more than 70 years, and a bridge from Drayton Park to Emirates Stadium is named in his honour.

A statue at the end of the bridge is a nod to the chance meeting the 11-year-old Friar had with Arsenal manager George Allison in 1945, while playing football outside Highbury with his friends.

As Sam Dean wrote earlier today, finishing the story: “Allison was so impressed by Friar’s enthusiasm that he told him to report to his office at 9am the next day. Friar did as he was instructed and his reward was a job offer: he became a messenger at the stadium on match days. He was paid 12 and a half pence per week.”

Friar was a long-serving member of the Arsenal board, before stepping back in 2020 and becoming life president.

Arsenal’s players will wear black armbands.

A post shared by Sam Dean (@samjdean_tel)

After signing his new Arsenal contract last week, Mikel Arteta described May’s Champions League final defeat as “poison in his veins,” and last season’s campaign demonstrated the benefits of finishing top of the league phase.

Arsenal enjoyed home second legs all the way through to the final after winning eight from eight, and in a 50:50 draw they fell into a considerably kinder bracket.

Sometimes it can be hard to gauge the importance of these league-phase matches, but Arteta will strive for another perfect record to give Arsenal the best possible chance of going deep in the competition again.

Fixtures against Bayern Munich and Real Madrid are likely to determine whether Arsenal finish in the top two, but there is still a job to be done against Lille this evening.

Arsenal have played against 10 different French opponents in European competition but have never faced Lille, who are managed by Davide Ancelotti, son of five-time Champions League winner Carlo.

Lille sell their best players every summer. After finishing third in Ligue 1 last season they lost Ayyoub Bouaddi and Matias Fernandez-Pardo to Manchester City and Newcastle United for a combined £130m. They have claimed 10 points from their first five league games of the season and led Paris St-Germain 2-0 before being pegged back in stoppage time.

Leading the line for Lille is 40-year-old Olivier Giroud, who scored 105 Arsenal goals in 235 appearances between 2012 and 2018. After leaving the Emirates, Giroud went on to score against Arsenal for Chelsea in the 2019 Europa League final, but he can still expect a warm reception.

Arsenal’s home record in the Champions League has been formidable since they returned to the competition under Arteta in 2023. They have won all 11 home group-stage or league-phase matches, conceding just three goals (two of those were shipped against Kairat Almaty in a dead rubber).

Arteta’s scope for rotation has been reduced by injuries to Piero Hincapie and Martin Zubimendi, but tonight’s game should offer Eberechi Eze and Viktor Gyokeres a chance to impress, while Jurrien Timber needs minutes to build his fitness.

#1328. Why Juventus had to register Ekhator and not Zhegrova in UEFA squad list changes

Juventus have added Jeff Ekhator to their UEFA squad list in place of injured captain Manuel Locatelli, and the competition’s registration rules decided it ahead of Edon Zhegrova.

According to TuttoMercatoWeb, the Bianconeri have finally replaced Locatelli, who had knee surgery on his meniscus in September and isn’t expected back until next year. Ekhator returned to the squad for Sunday’s 2-0 win over Napoli after a long injury lay-off.

On form, Zhegrova would have been the obvious choice. The winger has looked sharper in recent weeks and is one of Luciano Spalletti’s few fit attacking options, but he isn’t eligible.

UEFA requires every 25-man A list to include a minimum number of locally trained players: four trained at the club itself and up to four trained at other clubs in the same country.

Locatelli, who came through the youth system at Milan, counts as one of Juve’s association-trained players. That means he can only be swapped for a player in the same category.

Ekhator, a product of Genoa’s academy, fits that requirement. Zhegrova had never played in Italy before joining Juventus, so he would have taken one of the 17 unrestricted places, and those are already full.

#1327. Premier League: Man City Facing New Charges After Guilty Verdict

Manchester City are currently going through the appeal process after being found guilty of 114 breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations. But things could still get worse for the Citizens.

The Premier League announced in September that City had been found guilty of artificially inflating sponsorship deals during the nine years from 2009 to 2018.

City have maintained their innocence and the outcome of the appeal process is expected in the coming months. However, The Independent is now reporting that multiple executives want further investigations.

The Premier League are said to be facing a 'dilemma' as English football chiefs are pushing for further investigations into Man City's conduct.

More specifically, they are asking questions about the years that followed 2018. It is believed that directors are questioning whether the inflated sponsorship deals simply stopped in 2018, despite commercial income appearing to remain at the same level.

Manchester City could be in hot water with UEFA if they fail in their appeal against the Premier League's 115 financial charges.

In the original investigation, the Premier League found that Man City and the Abu Dhabi-based sponsors were 'related parties'. If it was proven that was still the case after 2018, then there would be a basis for further sanctions related to the seasons that followed.

The ongoing legal case began in 2023, when the Premier League accused the Manchester-based club of breaking115 financial charges after documents were leaked.

Now, executives don't believe the period after 2018 haven't been addressed adequately. However, the English top flight has taken a stance of not addressing the court case until it has reached a conclusion.

Potential punishments have been widely discussed since the guilty verdict. They have included large fines, transfer bans, titles being stripped, relegation and points deductions.

According to Football Insider, a single-season points deduction is the 'likely' course of action if the charges stick after City's appeal. The number of points is reported to be 'around 40 to 50 points'.

How much money Manchester City may need to pay 38 clubs in lost Premier League prize money

Previously, talkSPORT host and former footballer Alan Brazil claimed he'd been told a single-season points deduction was the punishment City would be handed. However, he claimed 60 points would be taken from them.

He said: "I’m hearing a 60-point deduction, which will please people and still give City a chance of surviving.

"I don’t know whether it’s this season. I can’t see how that can be this season because of the timing, when they get it through it’ll be too late. "Is it next season? But they are talking about a 60-point deduction."

#1326. Allegri: ‘Napoli’s Champions League fate is in our hands, but the league is more important’

Massimiliano Allegri insists Napoli’s Champions League fate is still in their own hands, but warned that turning their league form around matters more.

With quotes via TuttoMercatoWeb, the Napoli coach spoke at the Estádio do Dragão on Tuesday, before Wednesday’s game against Porto, which kicks off at 21:00 CET [20:00 GMT].

Allegri is back in the dugout after a two-match Serie A ban. During it, Napoli won 4-1 at Monza and lost 2-0 at Juventus, leaving them 10th on 14 points. In Europe, they have three points from three games after defeats in their first two matches and a 4-3 win over Bodø/Glimt.

He opened by paying tribute to Tenerife striker Jesús de Miguel, who died at 30 after a collision with Andorra goalkeeper Owono during a match in Spain. “First of all, I’d like to offer my condolences to the family of Jesús de Miguel for this tragic accident to a young man, before a footballer, who lost his life,” he said.

“Tomorrow’s game is difficult, because Porto have won 10 in a row in the league, and they’ve played some good games in the Champions League too. As for us, talking is of little use, we need to put in a good performance. In the Champions League, our destiny is in our hands, because with 10 points we’d reach the play-offs at least. But then there’s the league to sort out, and that’s the most important thing.”

“Tomorrow isn’t the last chance. With 10 points you go to the play-offs. Tomorrow is an important game. Manchester is an important game but almost impossible. We’ll fight for qualification against Club Brugge, Viking and Sabah,” Allegri said.

He denied the injury crisis takes any pressure off. “It doesn’t take any pressure off, because it’s an important Champions League game against a strong team. Right now there’s no need to talk and explain. There’s only the need to act, to work, to get the injured players back and turn this negative period into a positive one.”

On Rasmus Højlund and Kevin De Bruyne, he said: “Højlund’s fever has gone. De Bruyne will train today, and afterwards we’ll see if he’s available for tomorrow.”

Asked about fears of a repeat of the season Napoli finished 10th, Allegri said: “Right now it’s time to act, not to talk. It’s not an easy moment. We’ve had mixed results and haven’t yet managed to win two league games in a row. But what’s certain is that we have to keep working, get back all the players who will return after the international break, and try to turn things around in the league, where there will be time and space to recover. In the meantime, we’re thinking about tomorrow, there’s a game to play.”

He returned Francesco Farioli’s praise. “I think Farioli, a young coach, has already achieved good results, both in the Netherlands and in Portugal. He has a very important career ahead of him.”

On the threat Porto pose at home: “We know Porto are very aggressive at home, and they have technical, physical and high-quality players. When we have the ball we’ll need to be good technically, and when we don’t we’ll need to defend well, which is something we’ve done less this season.”

Asked whether Porto would press with fewer players or match Napoli’s numbers, he said: “I don’t know, it depends on what Farioli decides. Whether it’s numbers even or an extra man, you have to behave in two completely different ways.”
